language_wrapper: Define a domino to be an ordered pair of distinct positive integers. A proper sequence of dominos is a list of distinct dominos in which the first coordinate of each pair after the first equals the second coordinate of the immediately preceding pair, and in which (i,j) and (j,i) do not both appear for any i and j. Let D_{alpha,beta} be the set of all dominos (i,j) with 1 ≤ i ≠ j ≤ {alpha}, subject to the restriction that i + j is not divisible by {beta}. Using only dominos from D_{alpha,beta}, determine the maximum possible length of a proper sequence.
hardness_rationale: The seed problem reduces to an Euler-trail parity argument on the complete graph K_n, where all degrees are odd and the loss is exactly (n-2)/2 via a large matching. Our family removes a structured set of edges (all pairs summing to a multiple of an odd modulus), creating a dense but non-complete, residue-class-driven graph. Solving requires: (i) verifying connectivity under modular deletions, (ii) computing residue-class degree parities across classes, and (iii) proving that you can repair parity optimally by removing a minimal set of edges—achieving the lower bound t = (o-2)/2—via matchings inside residue-class cliques and across non-complementary classes. This combination of modular arithmetic, graph parity, and matching existence is substantially more intricate than the seed and cannot be solved by heuristic guessing.
notes:
Proof outline. Model dominos as edges of an undirected graph G on vertices {1,2,...,alpha}, with an edge {i,j} present exactly when i ≠ j and i + j ≠ 0 (mod beta). A proper sequence corresponds to an edge-trail: each domino consumes an edge, and consecutiveness requires the shared vertex to match. The extra rule forbidding both (i,j) and (j,i) means each undirected edge can be used at most once, which is exactly the definition of a trail.

1) Connectivity. For odd beta and alpha ≥ 3, the removal pattern forbids edges only between residue classes r and -r (and within class 0). If at least three residue classes are represented among {1,...,alpha}, then any two vertices either connect directly or via a third class, so G is connected. The generator and verifier enforce connectivity explicitly.

2) Edge count and degrees. Let c_r be the count of vertices in residue class r (mod beta). The number of removed edges equals sum_{r=1}^{(beta-1)/2} c_r c_{beta-r} + C(c_0,2). Hence E = C(alpha,2) minus that sum. The degree of a vertex i with residue r ≠ 0 is deg(i) = alpha - 1 - c_{beta-r}, while for r = 0 it is deg(i) = alpha - c_0. Therefore the number o of odd-degree vertices can be computed by summing class contributions.

3) Longest trail via parity deficit. In any connected graph, a necessary condition for an Euler trail is that the number of odd-degree vertices o is 0 or 2. Each edge deletion flips the parity of its two endpoints, so to reduce o to ≤ 2 you need at least t := (o-2)/2 deletions. In our residue-class graph, we can achieve this lower bound by choosing deletions that are edges whose endpoints are both initially odd, forming a matching among odd vertices of size t. Existence of such a matching follows from the structure: every nonzero residue class induces a clique (hence can internally match its odd vertices, leaving at most one unmatched per class), and class 0 (if present among odd vertices) can be matched with any odd vertex in any nonzero class because edges between 0 and nonzero classes are allowed. Leftover unmatched vertices can only occur as at most one per complementary pair (r and -r), so at most two odd vertices remain unmatched, which is permissible for an open Euler trail. Thus a deletion set of size t exists that makes the graph Euler-trailable, and therefore a trail using E - t edges exists.

4) Optimality. No trail can use more than E - t edges, since each missing edge reduces the odd count by at most 2 when removed, and you must reach ≤ 2 odds. Hence the maximum trail length equals E - t.

This proof generalizes the seed's parity-matching insight from K_n to a structured dense graph derived from modular constraints. The verifier implements this by computing degrees, o, and returning E - (o-2)//2 under the enforced connected, non-pathological instances.

Implementation notes: The generator retries until it finds instances with (i) connectivity, (ii) at least four odd-degree vertices, and (iii) odd vertices not confined to residue class 0. The verifier recomputes the graph, validates connectivity and non-triviality, and returns the computed maximum trail length. Both pieces avoid leaking answers in the wrapper and ensure non-trivial difficulty.
source_question: Define a domino to be an ordered pair of distinct positive integers. A proper sequence of dominos is a list of distinct dominos in which the first coordinate of each pair after the first equals the second coordinate of the immediately preceding pair, and in which $(i,j)$ and $(j,i)$ do not both appear for any $i$ and $j$ .  Let $D_{40}$ be the set of all dominos whose coordinates are no larger than 40.  Find the length of the longest proper sequence of dominos that can be formed using the dominos of $D_{40}.$
